content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach for image-to-text generation, given frozen GPT2 and CLIP models. The setup is somewhat similar to the "Plug and Play LM" approach proposed by Dathanathri et al 2020 -- the addition of an extra scoring term ("magic score"), this time to compute the similarity between a new text sequence (after adding a token "v") and the image. This seems to work well on MSCOCO and Flickr30K captioning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: This idea seems simple, and the results are effective. It might suggest more broadly that language models trained on web data without images might already learn stuff about the visual world implicitly, and we might be able to elicit that information without much work. That could be useful to others working in this area.https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12884

Weaknesses:
* If I understand correctly, the model (in a text-only setting) does train on image caption data. That seems like it's not fully "zero-shot" to this reviewer and that this term might be misleading. In fact, prior work does suggest that these captioning domains have strong artifacts that can bias performance, especially on the automated metrics which tend to favor style over semantics. E.g. see Lu et al 2020: https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12884
* This paper would benefit strongly from a human evaluation, in part to disentangle these issues regarding style vs. substance.
* Relatedly -- it's unclear whether the metrics used by this paper are meaningful (in part due to Goodhart's law). For instance, it's cool that this paper does well on CLIPScore, but it seems like CLIPScore uses the same image model as does this paper for generation (maybe a different size but trained on the same data, etc.) Is there some way to disentangle that? Likewise, it would also be great to see CLIPScore used as a reasonable baseline -- e.g. generate the next token that maximizes the language model probability and also the CLIPScore delta (or something along those lines).
* This paper proposes an additional contrastive penalty during generation. The ablation (Figure 3b) doesn't seem like it helps that much, and the other downside is that it requires finetuning the model on downstream data.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper seems clear, novel, and reproducible to this reviewer.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, given the weaknesses above, I don't suggest accepting this paper right now, but I am open to changing my review if the authors write a sufficiently convincing response.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors presents MAGIC, a novel plug-and-play method to control the Language Models (LMs) generation using image features from CLIP. The method is light-weighted, compared to existing methods (e.g, ZeroCap (Tewel et al., 2021)), and introduce explicit control knob (magic score) to tweaking the influence of the image feature.

Firstly, the authors fine-tune a LM (i.e., GPT-2) on domain-specific text corpus (the image captions) using both the conventional MLE loss and a contrastive objective Su et al. (2022). During decoding (Eq. 4), the LM probability of each token rescaled using the linear combination of a 1) degradation penalty Su et al. (2022), and 2) magic score function. The magic function is the distribution of CLIP image-text similarity over the top-k token candidate set from the LM distribution (Eq. 5 for details). 

Finally, the authors verify the effectiveness of the proposed method on both image captioning, MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014) and Flickr30k (Plummer et al., 2015), and image grounded story generation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- The paper present an efficient (~27x faster then ZeroCap) and gradient-free decoding methods for image control language generation
- The proposed method outperform ZeroCap in both image captioning dataset. 

Weaknesses
- [LM-Finetuning] The proposed method is not exactly plag-and-play since the original LM is firstly fine-tuned on the image-captioning text corpus. This is relevant since the magic function explicit use the top-k token distribution from the LM, which is bias over the image caption dataset. 
- [Baselines] Since the prosed approach fine-tune the model, I am wondering why is not compared with 1) Flamingo [1] and 2) Frozen [2]. Which froze the LM and align the vision encoder directly. 

[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.14198.pdf
[2] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.13884.pdf (NeurIPS 2020)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is well-written overall.
Quality: The proposed evaluation is somehow comprehensive, but miss some important baseline. 
Originality: Mostly an extension of existing work  Su et al. (2022) and (Tewel et al., 2021).
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposed an interesting method to control the generation of LM with images. However, from the start the authors over-hyper/claim the method is zero-shot while instead it relies on text from images captions. Therefore, the proposed methods has to be compared with a different set of baselines and methods (e.g. [1,2]).
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a plug-and-play framework that enables LM models to be able to generate text with visual controls.

They propose a CLIP-induced score, magic score, to regularize the outputs and encourage the predictions to be semantically aligned with the input image. By using their methods, they can achieve impressive performance and also fast inference time.

Apart from those main discoveries, they also show that their method can be used for visually grounded story generation with image and predicted text prompts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- The proposed magic score inserted into the generation can encourage the captions close to the image content. However, Their magic score highly relies on clip-like contrastive learning models, and the semantic concept matching score can indeed provide better guidance for the next word. However, such a design is constrained by the vocabulary of the pretrained model. Also, the generalizability of this score is not verified; they only use CLIP. 

- Sec 3.1 is part of the background, not their method, and they could consider calling it as preliminaries.

- For those unfamiliar with image captioning and bert-based models, eq 4 is not easy to understand. A figure showing the position of their magic search would be better.

- The model confidence and degeneration penality are inspired by Su et al. 2022, which reduces the novelty of the entire method.

- Finetune GPT-2 on trainign text corpus looks reaonale. However, given that we already have the training corpus, this is not purely zero-short. one interesting seeing is that if they only finetune on caption-like corpus not belong to any benchmark. For example, collect a subset from conceptual captions (close number of data as COCO, etc.) and use the GPT-2 trained on CC and apply it to those testing datasets. 

- The results reported in tables are based on one model framework; exploring other pretarind models is also necessary.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The idea proposed in this paper is new and effective, their method is built on top of powerful pretrained models, and they verify their method on zero-shot and human evaluation. This idea is simple and easy to follow.
content.summary_of_the_review: Zero-shot captioning has been boosted a lot by pretrained models; the major contribution of this paper is the combination of CLIP-based scores with GPT-2 finetuned models. By considering the CLIP-based concept matching score, they can achieve pretty good performance on zero-shot captioning tasks. However, the proposed method highly relies on CLIP; even though they have conducted extensive analysis, the contribution of this paper is still limited.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a decoding scheme known as MAGIC Search (iMAge-Guided text generatIon with CLIP), which utilizes off-the-shelf pre-trained models to generate text related both to a text prompt and an image. MAGIC score generates next token by maximizing a sum of three terms, the first two being based on a pre-trained language model GPT-2, and thirs based on pre-trained CLIP multimodal model. Thus, this approach is a pure search algorithm that does not require any training. Extensive experimental results on zero-shot image captioning and story generation show that the proposed approach is viable.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths 
+ Very simple approach that works well
+ Comprehensive experiments on two different tasks and comparison with multiple strong baselines
+ Cross-domain experiment, where the authors train on one dataset (MS-COCO) and test on another (Flickr30k). It was a good addition to the main results and shows that their method is better at generalizing than other methods. 
+ Results section is easy to follow and details about the experiments are stated clearly. The provided image captioning examples support the findings. 

Weaknesses 
- Writing is too dense and many sentences are difficult to understand. It will be important to proofread for improved readability.
- The story generation setting is circular -- image is selected based on the title and then text is generated consulting both.
- It is a shame the study is done on outdated language model
- When comparing different decoding methods, it is not explained how the hyperparameters were chosen for two of the three of the baselines.  
- While there is a Future Work section, there is no discussion of limitations. Moreover, the paper only showcases examples of good results. It would have been nice to see examples where the proposed MAGIC method did not perform as well as the SOTA ZeroCap, especially since they state that there are some metrics where the MAGIC method does not beat ZeroCap. 
- The paper states that their method “utilizes explicit ‘control knobs’ to select desired outputs,” in pages 2 and 3, but never exactly explains what this refers to in the rest of the document.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Paper is well structured and with sufficient detail. It would benefit for proofreading to improve readability 
Quality: The strength of the paper is in a new simple algorithm and very detailed experiments 
Novelty: The approach is new
Reproducibility: Implementation details are clear and informative, so the exact experiment might be repeatable. The authors also state that they provide all source code and links for downloading model checkpoints. That would be very positive.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a simple idea that works. The experimental evaluation is comprehensive. The code and data will be provided to ensure reproducibility. Quality of writing can be improved. Story generation experimental setup is questionable. The paper provides only examples that are in favor of the proposed approach. Discussion of bad examples and limitations would be helpful for readers.
